overview.text: Rwanda is a hilly, landlocked country in central Africa, bordered by Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its capital is Kigali. Hutu, Tutsi, and Twa communities have long been part of its history. After independence in 1962, Tutsi people faced discrimination and repeated violence. In 1994, extremist leaders of the Hutu-led government organized genocide against the Tutsi and also killed Hutu opponents. The killings followed the shooting down of President Juvénal Habyarimana’s plane, but responsibility for that attack remains disputed. The Rwandan Patriotic Front ended the genocide after capturing Kigali and overthrowing the government.

key_facts.text: Rwanda is landlocked and borders Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Kigali is Rwanda’s capital.
Rwanda gained independence in 1962.
The 1994 genocide targeted Tutsi people and Hutu opponents of the extremists.
The Rwandan Patriotic Front ended the genocide by capturing Kigali and overthrowing the government.

overview.text: RMS Titanic was a White Star Line ocean liner built for transatlantic travel. It departed Southampton on 10 April 1912 on its first voyage toward New York, stopping at Cherbourg in France and Queenstown in Ireland. Late on 14 April, it struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic and sank early on 15 April. The ship carried only 20 lifeboats, with room for fewer people than were aboard, and some boats left underfilled. About 1,500 passengers and crew died. The sinking became one of the best-known maritime disasters and exposed serious gaps in the safety arrangements of a large passenger liner. Its wreck was found in 1985.

key_facts.text: RMS means Royal Mail Ship.
Titanic’s maiden voyage began at Southampton on 10 April 1912.
It called at Cherbourg and Queenstown before entering the Atlantic.
The iceberg collision occurred late on 14 April; Titanic sank on 15 April 1912.
It carried 20 lifeboats, and approximately 1,500 people died.
The wreck was located in 1985.

overview.text: The Iranian Revolution of 1979 ended the monarchy of Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi and led to an Islamic Republic. Demonstrations, strikes, and opposition to political repression weakened the shah’s government during 1978. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, a prominent opponent in exile, returned to Tehran on 1 February 1979 after the shah had left Iran. The monarchy collapsed later that month. A referendum in March approved an Islamic republic, and a new constitution placed major authority with a supreme leader. The movement drew support from religious, liberal, and leftist opponents of the shah, but the political system that emerged was dominated by Khomeini and his allies. Its effects reshaped Iran’s government and foreign relations.

key_facts.text: Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi left Iran on 16 January 1979.
Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile on 1 February 1979.
The monarchy collapsed in February 1979.
A March 1979 referendum approved an Islamic republic.
The constitution gave supreme powers to Khomeini as supreme leader.

overview.text: Nazi concentration camps were detention sites operated outside normal judicial protections in Germany and its occupied territories from 1933 to 1945. The first camps imprisoned political opponents; Dachau, opened in 1933, became a model for the SS-run system. Prisoners later included Jews and many other people persecuted by Nazi rule. During World War II, the system expanded and exploited forced labor, while many prisoners died from abuse, starvation, disease, and murder. Concentration camps must be distinguished from killing centers built chiefly for mass murder on arrival. Auschwitz-Birkenau combined both functions, but sites such as Treblinka were killing centers rather than formal concentration camps. This distinction helps explain how the Nazi camp network operated.

key_facts.text: Dachau opened in March 1933 for political prisoners.
Concentration-camp imprisonment generally bypassed judicial trial and review.
The SS centralized management of the concentration-camp system.
Forced labor became a major purpose of camps during World War II.
Most killing centers, including Treblinka, were not formally concentration camps; Auschwitz-Birkenau was a major exception.

overview.text: The Iran hostage crisis began on 4 November 1979, when revolutionary students seized the United States embassy in Tehran after Iran’s revolution. They held American diplomatic personnel, and Ayatollah Khomeini’s government supported the action. The seizure followed the admission of the exiled shah to the United States for medical treatment. Early releases and escapes reduced the number held throughout the crisis; 52 remained at its end. President Jimmy Carter’s government sought their release through negotiations and a failed military rescue attempt in April 1980. The Algiers Accords provided the final agreement, and the hostages were released on 20 January 1981, ending 444 days of captivity.

key_facts.text: Students seized the U.S. embassy in Tehran on 4 November 1979.
The crisis lasted 444 days.
Six U.S. employees escaped Iran with Canadian help in January 1980.
The April 1980 U.S. rescue mission failed.
The final 52 hostages were released on 20 January 1981 after the Algiers Accords.

overview.text: French people are the citizens and national community of France, a country whose modern history includes the 1789 Revolution and successive republics. French identity is civic as well as cultural: today the republic states that sovereignty belongs to citizens as a whole and that their rights do not depend on wealth, gender, or religion. French is the republic’s official language, although people in France have varied backgrounds and traditions. During the French Revolution, the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen made equality before the law and national sovereignty central political ideas. French people also shaped events abroad: the Marquis de Lafayette served with the American forces in the Revolutionary War.

key_facts.text: The French Republic describes itself as indivisible, secular, democratic, and social.
French is France’s official language.
The 1789 Declaration stated that sovereignty rests in the nation.
The Declaration affirmed equality before the law.
The French Marquis de Lafayette fought with American forces in the Revolutionary War.

overview.text: Vladimir Putin is a Russian politician and former Soviet intelligence officer who has dominated Russia’s government since 1999. Born in Leningrad in 1952, he worked for the KGB, including in East Germany, and later headed Russia’s Federal Security Service. Boris Yeltsin appointed him prime minister in 1999; Putin became acting president when Yeltsin resigned, then won the 2000 presidential election. He served two presidential terms, was prime minister while Dmitry Medvedev held the presidency from 2008 to 2012, and returned to the presidency in 2012. He remained Russia’s president in 2026. His long rule has made him central to the study of post-Soviet Russia and its foreign policy.

key_facts.text: Putin was born in Leningrad in 1952.
He worked for the Soviet KGB and later headed Russia’s FSB.
Yeltsin appointed Putin prime minister in 1999.
Putin served as president from 2000 to 2008 and as prime minister from 2008 to 2012.
He returned to the presidency in 2012 and was still president in 2026.

overview.text: Roman coinage was the minted currency used across the Roman Republic and Empire. Coins moved through markets, taxes, and military pay, and their designs carried messages about rulers and public power. The denarius was a common silver coin; a surviving example shows the emperor Maximinus Thrax and a personification of Providence. A bronze sestertius of Trajan places his portrait on one side and a bridge on the other. These objects show why coins are valuable historical evidence: their metal, inscriptions, portraits, and reverse images can identify rulers and reveal what authorities wished to advertise. Coin types and metal content changed over time, especially amid economic strains in the third century.

key_facts.text: The denarius was a standard Roman silver coin used to pay soldiers.
A 236 CE silver denarius depicts Emperor Maximinus Thrax.
A bronze sestertius of Trajan shows his portrait and a bridge.
Roman rulers used coin portraits to publicize their authority.
Some third-century Roman coinage was debased, with less silver than its stated denomination implied.

overview.text: The Cuban Missile Crisis was an October 1962 confrontation that brought the United States and Soviet Union close to nuclear war. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed with Cuba’s Fidel Castro to place nuclear missiles on the island, partly to deter another U.S. invasion attempt. American U-2 photographs revealed missile sites under construction. President John F. Kennedy announced a naval “quarantine” to stop further weapons deliveries and demanded removal of the missiles. After tense public and private exchanges, Khrushchev agreed to withdraw them; the United States pledged not to invade Cuba and privately agreed to remove missiles from Turkey. The crisis showed how quickly Cold War rivalry could escalate and encouraged later efforts to improve superpower communication.

key_facts.text: The crisis occurred in October 1962.
A U-2 flight photographed Soviet missile sites in Cuba on 14 October.
Kennedy announced a naval quarantine on 22 October.
Khrushchev publicly agreed to remove the missiles on 28 October.
The settlement included a U.S. non-invasion pledge and a private understanding about U.S. missiles in Turkey.

overview.text: The October Crisis was a political emergency in Quebec, Canada, in 1970. Two cells of the Front de libération du Québec, a militant independence group known as the FLQ, kidnapped British trade commissioner James Cross and Quebec cabinet minister Pierre Laporte. Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau’s government invoked the War Measures Act on 16 October, claiming an “apprehended insurrection.” The act gave authorities sweeping powers and suspended civil liberties, provoking lasting debate about the government’s response. Laporte was killed; Cross was later released after negotiations. The crisis took place amid Quebec’s broader debate over independence, but the FLQ’s violent methods were distinct from the province’s peaceful political movements.

key_facts.text: FLQ members kidnapped James Cross on 5 October 1970.
A separate FLQ cell kidnapped Pierre Laporte on 10 October.
The federal government invoked the War Measures Act on 16 October.
The act suspended civil liberties and eased arrests and detentions.
Laporte was killed, while Cross was eventually freed through negotiations.
